title: the four weddings
hook: a father puts his daughter's hand in a young man's hand and says one sentence

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four weddings, part one. Two family trees recited aloud, and one wedding becomes four. Did you ask someone about the people who came before them? Today, the ceremony, and a week closes. Day five hundred eleven.

If you've been to a Hindu wedding, you may know the moment, though customs vary from family to family. The fire is lit in the middle of the canopy. The priest is chanting. And the bride's father stands, takes his daughter's hand, and places it in the groom's hand. Rooms full of noisy relatives go quiet for it. That moment has an echo in the Ramayana. Janaka, the king who found his daughter in a furrow, brings Sita to the altar, decked in jewels, and stands her across from Rama, by the fire.
screen: `THE FIRE UNDER THE CANOPY.` → `A FATHER, A HAND, A HAND.` → `JANAKA BRINGS SITA TO THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: Janaka speaks to Rama, and his words begin: iyam sita mama suta sahadharmachari tava. This is Sita, my daughter, your companion in dharma. Accept her. Take her hand in yours. She will be devoted to you, and will follow you always, like your shadow. Then he pours sacred water, and the gods say well done. Sahadharmachari is the key word. Saha, together. Dharma, the right way, duty, the path. Chari, one who walks. One who walks the path of dharma together with you. Not a possession, not a prize, though she was won by strength: a companion on the way. Janaka gives Urmila to Lakshmana, and his brother's daughters to Bharata and Shatrughna, with similar words. Then the four couples circle the fire, keeping it on their right, three times. Flowers fall from the sky, heavenly drums sound, and the apsaras dance. The next morning Vishvamitra says goodbye and leaves for the northern mountains. The sage who took two boys from their father's house leaves them married, with their father and brothers around them. Now the week, from the top. An empty hermitage, and Indra's disguise. Ahalya seen, honored, and hosting. Shatananda's question, and Sita rising from the furrow. The siege of the failed kings. The bow breaking like thunder. Two family trees recited. And today, four couples circling one fire, and a father's sentence about walking together.
screen: `THIS IS SITA, MY DAUGHTER.` · `SAHADHARMACHARI: WALKING TOGETHER.` · `FOUR COUPLES CIRCLE THE FIRE.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `IYAṂ SĪTĀ MAMA SUTĀ SAHADHARMACARĪ TAVA.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Bring to mind one person who walks some part of your path with you: a partner, a friend, a sibling, a colleague. Picture them beside you, not ahead or behind. On each breath in, feel their company. On each breath out, offer them yours. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Sahadharmachari, one who walks the path of dharma together with you. Janaka gives Sita to Rama as his companion in dharma, and four couples circle the fire together in Mithila.
Your line: a companion on the way. Today, share in someone else's small joy, a good grade, a new job, a finished project, as if it were yours too. Day five hundred eleven.

screen: `DAY 511 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK IN MITHILA, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: PARASHURAMA'S CHALLENGE.`

howItsDone: In Hindu weddings, the kanyadana, the father's giving of the bride's hand, and the circling of the sacred fire are central rites; some families recall Janaka's words to Rama when they explain them.

fork.setup: you're Janaka at the altar, giving your daughter's hand. what do you call her, in the text?
fork.reveal: sahadharmachari tava: your companion in dharma, one who walks the path with you.

original.note: Sanskrit sahadharmacarī: she who walks the path of dharma together with you. saha (together) + dharma + carī (one who walks).

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita is the prize for breaking the bow.
what it means: Janaka gives her as a companion in dharma, someone to walk the path with.
what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 73 has Janaka's verse beginning iyam sita mama suta, followed by the image of following like a shadow; the agni-pradakshina, circling the fire, is done three times.

notes: Week end: the teach looks back over days 505–511.
Janaka's verse quoted in Sanskrit transliteration (first half); the rest (accept her, take her hand, follow like a shadow) paraphrased. Confirm the half-verse and verse number.

The kanyadana rite is older than, and independent of, the Ramayana (grihya sutras); the hook now says the moment has an 'echo' in the epic rather than a scene 'behind it', and notes that customs vary. Janaka's words to Lakshmana are similar to, not identical with, his words to Rama, so 'the same words' became 'similar words'.
Whether all four couples receive similar words, and circle the fire three times together: paraphrased from sarga 73; confirm.
Carry action ('share in someone else's small joy') chosen to meet day 512's review question.
Editor review (2026-10-01): 'brought back four married men' was wrong (Vishvamitra took only Rama and Lakshmana, and he leaves rather than brings anyone back); rewritten. 'Often remembered' cut.
